extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers of Aristotle's ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Aristotelian criteria for Justice, Injustice, Equity, voluntariness, and the intellectual virtues (right reason, knowledge, practical wisdom) as presented in Nicomachean Ethics Books V–VI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is a mean between acting unjustly and being acted unjustly; it is a moral state aiming at producing the mean, whereas Injustice occupies both extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle emphasizes that justice differs from other virtues in that it aims at proportion and equality; justice produces balance between having more and having less. (Original phrasing: "just acting is a mean between acting unjustly and being acted unjustly... Justice ... is a mean state not after the same manner as the forementioned virtues, but because it aims at producing the mean, while Injustice occupies both the extremes.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as aptitude for proportionate distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the moral state by virtue of which the just person has the aptitude for practising the Just by moral choice and for making divisions between himself and another proportionably equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies both in distributing goods and in adjudicating rights; the just man neither gives himself more nor his neighbour less than the proportionate share. (Includes examples of dividing choice-worthy or hurtful things.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of Injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice is excess or defect of what is good or hurtful, a violation of the proportionate; it aims at producing excess or defect and therefore embodies both excess and defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injustice may manifest as taking more (excess) or giving less (defect) relative to the proportionate; in social contexts the direction of violation can vary case by case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of voluntariness for moral action
rubrics_metrics.description: An action becomes just or unjust only when it is voluntary; involuntary actions, done through ignorance or compulsion, do not make the agent just or unjust except accidentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntariness is defined as doing what is in one's power with knowledge (about the person, instrument, and likely result) and without compulsion. Examples: if another seizes one’s hand and strikes, the owner of the hand is not voluntary for that act; ignorance of the identity of the person struck can negate voluntariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of voluntary action
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary actions are those performed with knowledge and by the agent's own control — knowing whom you strike, with what, and the probable result, and not under compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle gives specific tests: knowledge of person, instrument, and result, absence of compulsion; contrasts with actions done through ignorance or by external force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: mistake vs. misadventure
rubrics_metrics.description: A misadventure occurs when harm comes contrary to all reasonable expectation (external cause); a mistake occurs when the origination of the cause rests with the agent though without viciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for assigning moral/blameworthy status to unintended harms. Examples: hitting someone you thought you would not hit (mistake) vs. utterly unforeseen harmful result (misadventure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation and character formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done with deliberate choice (after deliberation) confirm character; those done impulsively from passion may be unjust acts but do not necessarily make one a person of injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes between acting unjustly from anger or passion (unjust act but not confirmed unjust character) and acting unjustly from deliberate choice (which makes the agent a confirmed unjust and depraved person).

rubrics_metrics.name: Being unjustly dealt with requires lack of consent
rubrics_metrics.description: To be unjustly dealt with (to be a victim of injustice) the hurt must be against the wish of the person who is hurt; one cannot be unjustly dealt with with one's own consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases where a person suffers something voluntarily (e.g., gives away property) are not properly being unjustly dealt with. This clarifies moral status of consent and self-inflicted harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social justice requires mutual law and equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Social Justice arises among those who live in communion with a view to independence and who are free and equal either proportionately or numerically; Justice implies mutually acknowledged law and the possibility of injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where mutual legal relations and equality of ruling/rule exist, social justice and adjudication between just and unjust are possible; in relations lacking such equality (e.g., slave-owner) a different kind of justice applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different forms of justice by relation and origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice varies by relationship (social vs. domestic) and by origin (natural vs. conventional); some just relations are natural (have same force everywhere), others are conventional/enacted (vary by place or decree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: price or ransom fixed by convention; domestic justice (between husband and wife, parent and child) differs from social justice. Not all perceived variations imply absence of natural justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between abstract Just/Unjust and acts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between the abstract Just/Unjust (universals) and particular just/unjust acts: the universal is singular while acts are many, and an unjust thing in itself is not an unjust action until embodied voluntarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminological note: some Greek terms distinguish generic just acts vs corrective acts; moral responsibility depends on the act being voluntary and particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity as correction of general law
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity (the Equitable) is Just and even better than one form of Just (the law-based just) because it corrects cases where universal legal statements fail to apply rightly to particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity arises when law's necessary universality omits particular exceptions; the equitable agent corrects omissions as the lawgiver would have done if present. Example: law is universal but cannot cover every unique fact — a judge applying equity 'waives' the strict letter for justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of dealing unjustly solely by oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot properly deal unjustly by oneself in the full sense of being an unjust person because unjust action requires plurality (a wrong done to another), deliberate aggressive voluntariness, and falling under particular crimes which presuppose others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues conceptual and practical reasons: self-harm with consent is not injustice; unjust action implies some other party to be wronged; crimes like seduction or theft involve others by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative badness: doing injustice vs suffering injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Both doing injustice and suffering injustice are wrong (having more or less than the mean), but doing injustice towards others is worse, as it involves wickedness and blame, whereas suffering unjustly may be morally less blameworthy though possibly worse accidentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to medical evils: intrinsic severity differs from accidental greater harm; scientific definitions separate moral badness from contingent consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Reason and the mean in moral choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Men should choose the mean, neither excess nor defect, according to the dictates of Right Reason; Right Reason must be defined because mere exhortation to moderation is insufficient guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right Reason connects intellectual and moral faculties: moral choice requires both correct intellectual operation (deliberation) and right will; examples contrast knowing what is wholesome vs knowing how to administer remedies — analogous to knowing what is just vs how to enact it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of the rational soul and intellectual excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational soul divides into (a) that which apprehends necessary truths (knowledge) and (b) that which calculates and deliberates (the calculative). Excellence (virtue) of each part corresponds to its function and the truth it attains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle enumerates intellectual faculties (art, knowledge, practical wisdom, science, intuition) and links knowledge to necessary/eternal truths, teachability, and syllogistic demonstration; practical wisdom concerns deliberation about things that can be otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge concerns necessary and eternal things, is demonstrable syllogistically, is teachable, and is the product of induction (source of universals) and syllogistic reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes knowledge from opinion and supposition (which can err), and remarks on methods of teaching (induction → universal principles; syllogism → reasoning from those universals).
